findings.title: resolve() expiry check is inverted — live links are deleted, dead links are served
findings.description: The condition `if (Clock::now() < it->second.expires_at)` is true for NON-expired links, and in that branch the link is erased and false is returned. As written, resolving any valid link deletes it from the store and returns 404, while expired links fall through to hits++/return target. Resolve is the hot path for every redirect, so normal traffic destroys live links (data loss) and keeps serving expired ones.

findings.title: bearer_token dereferences nullptr when header has no space
findings.description: strchr(copy, ' ') returns nullptr when the Authorization header lacks a space (including the empty string handle() passes when the header is missing). `std::string(space + 1)` then computes nullptr+1 and reads from an invalid address, crashing the process on any such request.

findings.title: bearer_token copies unbounded header into 64-byte stack buffer
findings.description: std::strcpy(copy, header.c_str()) overflows `char copy[64]` for any Authorization header longer than 63 bytes, corrupting the stack. The request header is attacker-controlled.

findings.title: require_admin logic is wrong: admins are always rejected
findings.description: `if (session.role != "admin" || session.role != "owner")` — a role cannot equal both "admin" and "owner", so one side of the || is always true, so the function always returns false. Every admin request is rejected; contrast with the documented intent that admin sessions get through.

findings.title: verify() never checks session expiry — expired sessions stay valid forever
findings.description: The doc comment says verify returns nullptr once a session's lifetime has run out, but the loop only matches the token and returns the session unconditionally. expires_at is never compared against Clock::now(), so sessions live forever.

findings.title: top() sorts ascending and pads with default-constructed Links
findings.description: Two defects in one function: (1) the comparator `a.hits < b.hits` sorts least-followed first, so the leaderboard's 'most hits first' order is inverted; (2) `all.resize(n)` when n > all.size() appends n - size default-constructed Links (empty code, 0 hits) to the result instead of clamping.

findings.title: prune() erases through the loop iterator then increments it
findings.description: `for (auto it = links_.begin(); it != links_.end(); ++it) { ... links_.erase(it); }` — erase invalidates `it`, and the subsequent ++it is undefined behavior; elements are skipped and the loop can crash. Also the function returns `links_.size()` instead of `removed`, so the caller gets the post-prune map size, not the removal count the doc promises.

findings.title: page() computes end = all.size() + 1 and constructs an out-of-range iterator
findings.description: When the requested window runs past the end, `end` is set to `all.size() + 1`, and `std::vector<Link>(all.begin() + offset, all.begin() + end)` then forms an iterator one past the end — undefined behavior and a past-the-end read. (Negative offsets are likewise unchecked.)

findings.title: extend() revives expired links and does not add to expiry
findings.description: The doc says expiry is final and an expired link must never come back to life, and that ttl is pushed (added) out. The code sets `expires_at = Clock::now() + ttl` unconditionally: an expired link becomes valid again, and even a live link has its absolute expiry reset rather than extended by ttl.

findings.title: write_snapshot renames before the ofstream is flushed/closed
findings.description: `out << payload;` is immediately followed by std::rename while `out` is still open — the buffer may not be on disk, so the renamed snapshot.json can be empty or truncated despite the doc promising a crash-safe write. Additionally the fixed path /tmp/linkd-snapshot.json lets concurrent processes clobber each other, and the rename's return value is ignored (it also fails outright across filesystems, which also breaks the durability claim, and no fsync is done).

findings.title: Janitor erases from the map while iterating with ++it
findings.description: `for (auto it = store.all().begin(); it != store.all().end(); ++it) { ... store.all().erase(it); }` — erase invalidates the iterator before the loop increments it; behavior is undefined and entries are skipped or memory is corrupted. It also bypasses the store's own bookkeeping by erasing directly through the reference returned by all().

findings.title: warm_cache never joins its worker threads — std::terminate on return
findings.description: The doc promises the function returns only after every probe has finished, but no join() is ever called. The std::vector<std::thread> is destroyed at scope exit with joinable threads still in it, which calls std::terminate and aborts the process.

findings.title: check_targets reads one past the end of the vector
findings.description: `for (size_t i = 0; i <= links.size(); i++)` iterates to and including index links.size(); on the final iteration `links[links.size()]` is an out-of-bounds read (undefined behavior, potential crash).

findings.title: /stats divides by zero when the store is empty
findings.description: `g_store->total_hits() / g_store->size()` divides by store size with no zero check. With an empty store this is an integer division by zero and crashes the process on every /stats call.

findings.title: format_row returns a pointer to a dead stack buffer
findings.description: format_row returns `const char* row` where `row` is a local `char[128]`; the returned pointer dangles as soon as the function returns, and any caller printing/logging it reads uninitialized stack memory.

findings.title: last_code returns a string_view to a destroyed local
findings.description: `newest` is a local std::string and last_code returns std::string_view into it; the view dangles on return and any use of it reads freed stack memory. Additionally the function returns the lexicographically largest code (map ordering), not the most recently created link the doc promises.

findings.title: Cache leaks every Entry — entries_ holds raw pointers that are never deleted
findings.description: entries_ is std::map<std::string, Entry*>. No code path ever deletes an Entry: the destructor only calls entries_.clear(), erase() (line 50), get()'s expired branch (line 20), set() when overwriting an existing key (line 45) and set()'s eviction of the victim (line 39) all drop pointers without deleting. In a long-running service every cached entry leaks, so memory grows without bound.

findings.title: sweep() erases map entries while iterating with ++it
findings.description: erase(it) invalidates the iterator, then the for-loop does ++it — undefined behavior and skipped entries, so expiry sweeping can crash or silently fail to reclaim entries.

findings.title: validate() always returns true — bad configurations are never refused
findings.description: After collecting problems and logging them, the function falls through to `return true` with no `!problems.empty()` check. The documented startup guard is a no-op; callers (main ignores the return value too) will run with an invalid port/cache size/timeout.

findings.title: LINKD_TIMEOUT_MS / LINKD_CACHE_TTL_MS are milliseconds but parsed as seconds
findings.description: Both `Seconds{ms}` (timeout, line 25) and `Seconds{std::atoi(ttl)}` (cache TTL, line 29) interpret millisecond inputs as whole seconds, so LINKD_TIMEOUT_MS=5000 yields a 5000-second timeout instead of 5 seconds. Additionally, when ms == 0 the code logs 'keeping default' but still assigns Seconds{0}, contradicting its own message and tripping (well, with a fixed validate, failing) validation.

findings.title: by_owner uses substring match instead of exact ownership
findings.description: `pair.second.owner.find(owner) != std::string::npos` matches any owner whose name contains `owner` as a substring, returning other users' links (the doc promises exactly this owner's links). A short query like "a" matches almost every owner.

findings.title: Metrics::errors_ is never initialized
findings.description: resolved_ and created_ have default member initializers but errors_ does not. Metrics has no user-provided constructor, so errors() reads an indeterminate value and /stats reports a garbage error count.

findings.title: success_rate() integer-divides to 0 (or 100) every time
findings.description: `used / links_.size() * 100` divides two ints before multiplying, so the fraction is 0 whenever fewer than all links were hit, and exactly 100 only when all were. Partial hit rates are reported as 0%.

findings.title: utilization() integer-divides and divides by zero when limit is 0
findings.description: `entries_.size() / limit_ * 100` always yields 0 for any non-full cache (e.g. 512/1024), and if limit_ is 0 (accepted by config, since validate only rejects negative) it is a division by zero and crashes.

findings.title: cache eviction picks the lexicographically smallest key, not the LRU entry
findings.description: The map is ordered by code, so `entries_.begin()` is the alphabetically first code, not the least-recently-used entry the doc and the `used` timestamps promise. Also, when `code` already exists, the fullness check evicts an innocent entry and then overwrites the old one, which is additionally leaked.

findings.title: peek() reports expired entries as cached
findings.description: peek() only checks map membership and ignores entry->expires, so callers are told a code is cached even though get() would reject it. Expired entries are only removed on get/sweep.

findings.title: rename() validates `from` twice and never validates `to`
findings.description: `validate_code(from); validate_code(from);` is a copy-paste slip; the new code `to` is never validated, so a rename can install codes containing path separators, spaces, or arbitrary bytes (bypassing create's constraints) into the map and the CSV/terminal outputs.

findings.title: create() silently overwrites an existing link on code collision
findings.description: `links_[code] = link;` with an 8-hex-char random code doesn't detect a collision with a live link: the previous link's target/stats are silently destroyed, and quota is incremented again for the same slot. The caller gets a `Link*` that now points at the attacker-usable colliding code without any signal.

findings.title: remove() never decrements the owner's quota
findings.description: The doc promises remove gives the owner their quota slot back so a user who deletes a link can create another, but quota_ is not decremented; quota grows monotonically, diverging from the links map and permanently consuming slots.

findings.title: quotas() returns the internal map by reference despite documenting a snapshot
findings.description: The doc says the returned map is a snapshot whose mutation must not affect the store, but the function returns `std::map<std::string,int>&` aliasing quota_; any caller (e.g. count_for_owner's operator[], an admin handler) mutates live store state, and inserts phantom zero entries for unknown owners.

findings.title: import_all() is not atomic despite its contract
findings.description: The doc promises all-or-nothing, but validation and insertion happen in the same loop: if validate_code throws on link N of the batch, links 0..N-1 remain inserted. A failed import leaves the store with a partial batch.

findings.title: stop_janitor() never joins the thread
findings.description: stop_janitor only flips g_running (and the thread sleeps for a full interval first), leaks the std::thread, and any subsequent destruction of the store/cache can race with the still-running thread, which dereferences the captured references after they may be dead.

findings.title: Unguarded req.query.at(...) throws out of handlers on missing params
findings.description: create_link (lines 40-44), redirect (line 52), and the other handlers call req.query.at(...) without checking count(); a missing parameter throws std::out_of_range, which nothing in handle() catches, so the request kills the handler thread with an unhandled exception instead of a 400.

findings.title: File-open and write failures are silently ignored
findings.description: export_csv, archive_all and append_audit never check whether the ofstream opened or whether writes fail. A bad export dir or full disk produces a 'successful' empty export and a silently missing audit-log line, and report() in main.cpp will then happily serve the empty/missing file.

findings.title: count_for_owner inserts a zero entry for unknown owners
findings.description: store.quotas()[owner] uses operator[] on the live map, so merely querying the quota of an owner who has never created anything inserts a spurious 0 entry into the store's quota map (and report it if quotas are ever cleaned up or iterated).

findings.title: LINKD_FETCH_LIMIT is parsed and then discarded
findings.description: The parsed value is validated for positivity and then `(void)parsed;` — fetch_limit in the returned Config is always the default. Operators setting LINKD_FETCH_LIMIT get silently ignored.

findings.title: load_file accepts values without applying the same checks as the environment path
findings.description: cache_size from the file is parsed with std::atoi with no validation beyond what validate() (which currently always returns true) would do, and unknown keys are silently ignored — likely masking typos like `cachesize=`. Given validate is the only guard and it never fails, a bad file value flows straight into Cache (e.g. negative cache_size makes entries_.size() >= limit_ always true and utilization divide by zero/negative).

findings.title: Janitor erases from the map while iterating it (iterator invalidation)
findings.description: The janitor loop does `for (auto it = store.all().begin(); ...; ++it) { ... store.all().erase(it); }`. std::map::erase invalidates the erased iterator, so the `++it` in the loop increment is undefined behavior on the next iteration. Once any link has expired (i.e., every sweep after the first TTL window), the janitor thread walks off a dangling iterator, which corrupts the heap or crashes the process while it is simultaneously symbolizing/racing with request threads.

findings.title: Janitor thread mutates the store map concurrently with request handlers, with no synchronization
findings.description: start_janitor runs a loop that iterates `store.all()` and calls `erase` on it every interval, while handler threads concurrently execute Store::create/resolve/remove/import_all/prune/page etc. on the same std::map. std::map offers no thread-safe concurrent traversal+mutation: the tree structure can be torn mid-rebalance, leading to crashes, lost links, or corrupted red-black invariants. The same applies to the raw `std::map&` escape hatch in Store::all(), which hands the internal map to anyone. Interleaving: thread A (handler) is inside links_.find() during a lookup while thread B (janitor) erases a node; the found iterator/reference dangles and the subsequent it->second access is a use-after-free.

findings.title: stop_janitor sets a flag but never joins the thread; janitor can outlive the store/cache
findings.description: stop_janitor only sets g_running=false and returns immediately. The thread may still be sleeping in sleep_for(interval) or mid-sweep inside store/cache when the caller proceeds to tear down the Store/Cache (or the process exits). The captured references dangle and the thread is never joined (g_janitor is also leaked), so there is no ordering guarantee between 'janitor stopped touching the store' and 'store destroyed'. This is a classic shutdown-time use-after-free window.

findings.title: warm_cache spawns threads it never joins; cache written concurrently with no locking
findings.description: The docstring says it returns after every probe has finished, but the workers vector is destroyed at function exit with the threads still joinable — std::thread's destructor calls std::terminate, killing the process. Before that, all worker threads call cache.set() concurrently on the same Cache (entries_ map insert/erase and hits_ increment) with no synchronization, racing on the map structure and leaking entries overwritten via operator[].

findings.title: sweep() erases the current element while iterating
findings.description: `for (auto it = entries_.begin(); it != entries_.end(); ++it) { if (...) entries_.erase(it); }` — erase(it) invalidates `it`, and the loop's `++it` then advances a dangling iterator: undefined behavior. This runs on every janitor tick as soon as one cached entry has expired, so the cache janitor thread can crash or corrupt the entries_ map exactly when it is most needed.

findings.title: Cache is not thread-safe; janitor and handlers race on entries_, Entry and hits_
findings.description: Request threads call get()/set()/erase()/utilization()/stats() while the janitor thread concurrently calls sweep(). All of them mutate/read `entries_` (a plain std::map), Entry::used/expires fields, and the plain long `hits_`. Concurrent map insert/erase/find from multiple threads is undefined behavior; hits_++ from multiple threads loses updates; get() writes entry->used while another thread may be erasing that entry. Entries are also leaked (new Entry never delete'd) so long-running races compound.

findings.title: prune() erases map elements while iterating forward
findings.description: Same invalidation pattern as the janitor: `for (auto it = links_.begin(); it != links_.end(); ++it) { if (...) links_.erase(it); }`. Every call that removes at least one expired link increments a destroyed iterator — undefined behavior, ranging from a skipped element to a corrupted map or a segfault, and this function is the intended sweep mechanism for the store.

findings.title: Metrics counters are plain long incremented from all request threads
findings.description: add_resolved()/add_created() do resolved_++/created_++ on plain long members with no atomicity. handle() is invoked concurrently per request, so increments race: lost updates and, formally, a data race (undefined behavior). Readers (resolved(), created(), errors()) likewise read them without synchronization. errors_ is additionally never initialized.

findings.title: verify() returns a pointer into the sessions_ map; concurrent issue()/revoke() invalidate it and corrupt the map
findings.description: verify() hand-iterates sessions_ and returns `&pair.second`, which the caller (handle() in main.cpp and everything downstream) keeps using. Meanwhile another thread calling issue() inserts into sessions_ (rebalancing the tree while this thread traverses it) and revoke() erases a session — erasing the very element the pointer was returned from leaves the caller with a dangling Session*. std::map concurrent traversal + structural mutation is undefined behavior regardless of node stability, so even pointers to non-erased elements are not safely reachable during another thread's insert/erase.

findings.title: quotas() leaks a mutable reference to the internal quota_ map; callers read it unsynchronized while create/remove mutate it
findings.description: quotas() returns std::map<std::string,int>& to the private quota_ member, documented as 'a snapshot' but actually the live map. count_for_owner (worker.cpp) and admin_quotas (main.cpp) read it while other threads insert/erase in create() (quota_[owner]++) and remove() on the same map — a data race on the map structure with no external lock (main's handlers call these concurrently). Callers can also corrupt quota_ directly through the reference.

findings.title: Stack buffer overflow in bearer_token via Authorization header
findings.description: bearer_token() does std::strcpy(copy, header.c_str()) into char copy[64]. header is the raw HTTP Authorization header, fully attacker-controlled and arbitrarily long; anything over 63 bytes smashes the stack. It is called before authentication in handle(), so no credentials are needed. Additionally, if the header contains no space, strchr returns nullptr and 'space + 1' is undefined behavior.

findings.title: Session tokens are predictable (unseeded rand, 16 hex chars)
findings.description: issue() builds tokens from two std::rand() calls with %08x formatting, and rand() is never seeded anywhere, so the sequence is identical on every boot. An attacker who observes a few tokens (or brute-forces the small keyspace) can predict other users' session tokens and hijack sessions. Token entropy and source are both inadequate for an unguessable credential.

findings.title: verify() never checks expires_at; expired sessions never die
findings.description: Despite the doc comment promising rejection of expired tokens, verify() only compares token strings. Sessions are issued with a 12h expiry but remain valid forever, so a leaked token (logged, browser history, proxies) is usable indefinitely, and revocation windows never close on their own.

findings.title: Inverted expiry check in resolve(): live links deleted, dead links served
findings.description: if (Clock::now() < it->second.expires_at) erases the link and returns false, i.e. valid links are destroyed and reported missing, while expired links fall through and are served with hits incremented. Availability is destroyed for live links and the 'dead codes cannot be revived' invariant is inverted — expired, possibly malicious targets keep resolving.

findings.title: page() constructs vector range past end (heap out-of-bounds read)
findings.description: end is clamped to all.size() + 1 instead of all.size(), and the returned vector is built from [all.begin()+offset, all.begin()+end). The default caller (report) uses page(0, 1000), so any store with fewer than 1000 links produces an end iterator one past the end, reading out of bounds — UB, heap disclosure into the exported report, or a crash.

findings.title: by_owner() uses substring match, leaking other owners' links
findings.description: find(owner) != npos matches any owner whose name merely contains the query (e.g., 'ali' matches 'alice'), so a caller asking for their own links also receives links belonging to other users — an authorization/data-isolation failure on any endpoint backed by this lookup.

findings.title: Path traversal in export name: arbitrary file write and read
findings.description: export_csv builds path as dir + "/" + name + ".csv" with name taken straight from the HTTP query (report() passes req.query['name']). A value like '../../etc/cron.d/x' writes attacker-controlled CSV anywhere the service user can write (content includes attacker-influenced owner/target fields). The companion read_report (line 63) applies the same concatenation to open and return any *.csv on disk, so /report?name=../../etc/secret reads it back. No sanitization or confinement to dir exists.

findings.title: delete_link lets any authenticated user delete any link (IDOR)
findings.description: The handler ignores the session entirely and deletes by code from the query string. The comment claims the owner is taken from the authenticated session, but no such check exists; any logged-in user can enumerate/delete other users' links at will, destroying their data and links.

findings.title: Admin endpoint authorized by client-supplied 'x-admin: true' header
findings.description: /admin/quotas is gated solely on the caller sending the literal header x-admin: true. Any authenticated user can set that header and read the admin quota report; require_admin() exists but is never called. This is security-by-client-assertion, not access control.

findings.title: /report exports every owner's links to any authenticated user
findings.description: report() calls page(0, 1000) — the full store, unfiltered by owner — and writes/returns it as a CSV. Any valid token holder downloads every user's links, targets, and owner names, a bulk cross-tenant data disclosure. The export_csv comment even notes the report 'carries every owner's links'.

findings.title: warm_cache never joins workers: unsequenced threads on destroyed Cache + terminate
findings.description: workers.emplace_back(...) threads are captured by reference (&cache, &link — link is a reference into the caller's vector) and never joined or detached. When warm_cache returns, the vector<std::thread> is destroyed with joinable threads -> std::terminate; until then, concurrent cache.set() calls race on the shared map/entries_ with no synchronization, corrupting heap state.

findings.title: Passwords hashed with unsalted djb2
findings.description: hash_password() computes a 33-multiplier 64-bit hash (djb2) with no salt and no work factor. Any leak of the user table allows near-instant brute force and rainbow-table recovery of every password, and identical passwords hash identically (enabling correlation).

findings.title: Session tokens written to stdout logs
findings.description: issue() logs 'issued token <token> for <owner>'. Anyone with access to log files, log aggregation, or console scrollback obtains live bearer tokens (which also never expire, see verify()), enabling silent account takeover.

findings.title: Hardcoded fallback secret 'dev-secret-do-not-use'
findings.description: When LINKD_SECRET is unset, the service silently runs with a well-known compiled-in secret rather than failing closed. Any environment missing the variable (a common misconfiguration) uses a key an attacker already knows; the service gives no indication it is running with a guessable secret.

findings.title: create_link takes owner from query string, not the session
findings.description: The owner attribute (used for quotas, exports, and deletion ownership) is supplied by the caller as req.query['owner']. Any authenticated user can mint links attributed to arbitrary owners, exhausting their quota and poisoning their data/exports — a privilege/integrity issue the authenticated session cannot prevent.

findings.title: Open redirect in /out via unvalidated next parameter
findings.description: out() issues a 301 to whatever 'next' contains, with no allowlist or scheme check. Attackers can host links on this trusted domain that 302/301 victims to arbitrary (e.g. phishing) sites, abusing the service's reputation and any 'click counting' trust flows built on it.

findings.title: /stats divides by g_store->size() — crash on empty store
findings.description: long per_link = total_hits() / size() with a fresh store is integer division by zero, which crashes the process. Any authenticated caller can repeatedly DoS a newly started instance (e.g. right after deploy or after all links expire).

findings.title: archive_all writes per-owner files using the attacker-controlled owner as filename
findings.description: The output filename is dir + "/" + owner + ".csv", and owner originates from the create-link query string. An owner value like '../../etc/cron.d/x' (or with slashes/absolute path semantics via '..') makes archive_all overwrite arbitrary files the service user can write, with CSV content under partial attacker control.

findings.title: Snapshot written to predictable fixed /tmp path, never fsync'd
findings.description: write_snapshot always uses /tmp/linkd-snapshot.json with default open flags. On a shared host, a local attacker can pre-create/symlink that path to redirect the write and clobber other files the service user can write; and because the file is never fsync'd and rename() is used without directory sync, the 'crash-safe durable snapshot' guarantee does not actually hold — silent snapshot loss or corruption on power failure.

findings.title: Report file created with default (likely world-readable) permissions
findings.description: ofstream uses the process umask (commonly 022 → 0644). The comment states the report carries every owner's links and must be readable only by the service user, but nothing restricts the mode — other local users can read all owners' links and targets.

findings.title: CSV formula injection (unescaped fields starting with =, +, -, @)
findings.description: code/target/owner are emitted raw into CSV. The owner field is fully attacker-controlled (create_link ?owner=), so a value like '=cmd|"/c calc"!A1' or '+cmd|...' executes when a staffer opens the export in Excel/LibreOffice — code execution on the analyst's workstation and a classic spreadsheet-macro vector.

findings.title: format_row returns pointer to destroyed stack buffer
findings.description: row is a local char[128]; returning it as const char* leaves callers with a dangling pointer into a dead stack frame. Any read through it is undefined behavior — stale/garbage bytes or leaked stack contents can end up in output (and the snprintf content itself is uncontrolled if code/target are long).

findings.title: check_targets iterates past the end (off-by-one)
findings.description: for (size_t i = 0; i <= links.size(); i++) reads links[links.size()] on the final iteration — out-of-bounds read on std::vector, under ASan a crash, otherwise UB and potentially leaking adjacent heap memory into the 'first failure' result.

findings.title: Janitor erases map elements while iterating (UB)
findings.description: The janitor loop calls store.all().erase(it) and then ++it on the invalidated iterator — undefined behavior on every sweep that finds an expired entry; can skip entries, corrupt the map, or crash the janitor thread (taking down expiry enforcement silently).

findings.title: last_code returns string_view to a local that is destroyed
findings.description: newest is a local std::string; returning string_view of it leaves a dangling view on return. Any dashboard banner using it reads freed stack memory — UB, potential stack-data disclosure.

findings.title: extend() resurrects expired links
findings.description: Despite the contract 'an already-expired link stays expired; a dead code must never come back to life', extend() blindly sets expires_at = now + ttl for any existing entry, including long-dead ones. Expired/malicious targets become reachable again, breaking the expiry security invariant.

findings.title: Short-link codes from unseeded rand() are predictable
findings.description: Codes are sprintf('%08x', rand()) with no seeding, so the code sequence is deterministic from boot. Anyone can enumerate/predict valid codes and enumerate or access short links (and the shared rand stream also weakens session tokens).

findings.title: validate() always returns true — fail-open configuration gate
findings.description: The 'refuse to boot on bad config' check collects problems but returns true unconditionally, so port 0/99999, negative cache sizes, or non-positive timeouts all start anyway — pushing failures into runtime (e.g. division by zero in Cache::utilization when cache_size=0, or a dead service binding port 0).

findings.title: CORS allows any origin with credentials
findings.description: Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * combined with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true is an invalid, contradictory pair; browsers reject credentialed '*', but the intent is 'any site, with credentials' and non-browser clients ignore the distinction. Do not advertise credentials across origins you don't control.

findings.title: require_admin uses || so it can never grant admin
findings.description: session.role cannot equal both 'admin' and 'owner', so (role != "admin" || role != "owner") is always true and the function always returns false. It fails closed, but any future caller trusting it will lock out legitimate admins — and the intent was clearly &&.

findings.title: rename() validates 'from' twice and never validates 'to'
findings.description: Duplicate validate_code(from); the destination is unchecked, so arbitrary bytes (including separators/control chars) can be installed as a code, later flowing into CSV exports, caches and logs. The obvious intent was to validate 'to'.
